arXiv:2609.14235v1 [math.OC] 13 Sep 2026

Optimal Deterministic First-Order Oracle Complexity for Nonconvex-Concave Minimax Optimization

Siyu Pan ††thanks: Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia. Email: siyu.pan@sauder.ubc.ca.    Taoli Zheng ††thanks: RIKEN AIP. Email: taoli.zheng@riken.jp.    Jiajin Li ††thanks: Sauder School of Business, The University of British Columbia. Email: jiajin.li@sauder.ubc.ca.
September 13, 2026
Abstract

We study the deterministic first-order oracle complexity of smooth nonconvex-concave minimax optimization over a bounded convex dual domain. Let ℓ\ell denote the joint smoothness constant, D𝒴D_{\mathcal{Y}} the diameter of the dual domain, and Δ\Delta the initial gap. We prove that every deterministic first-order algorithm requires Ω⁡(ℓ2​D𝒴​Δ/ϵ3)\Omega(\ell^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta/\epsilon^{3}) oracle queries in the worst case to find an ϵ\epsilon-optimization-stationary point whenever ϵ≲min⁡{ℓ​D𝒴,ℓ​Δ}\epsilon\lesssim\min\{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}},\sqrt{\ell\Delta}\}. We then develop Tracked-FOAM, a first-order method that attains a matching upper bound, removing the logarithmic factor from previous upper bounds. Together, these results establish the optimal dependence on all problem parameters in the stated regime.

Key words. nonconvex minimax optimization, oracle complexity, lower bounds, first-order methods, convergence analysis

AMS subject classifications. 90C26, 90C47, 90C60

1 Introduction

We study the deterministic first-order oracle complexity of the smooth nonconvex-concave (NC-C) minimax problem

min𝒙∈𝒳⁡max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝒚),\min_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x};\bm{y}), (P)

where ff is jointly ℓ\ell-smooth and concave in 𝒚\bm{y}, 𝒳⊆ℝm\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} is a nonempty closed convex set, and 𝒴⊆ℝn\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is a nonempty compact convex set with diameter D𝒴D_{\mathcal{Y}}. Let Φ⁡(𝒙):=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝒙,𝒚)+ι𝒳​(𝒙)\Phi(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x};\bm{y})+\iota_{\mathcal{X}}(\bm{x}), where ι𝒳\iota_{\mathcal{X}} is the indicator function of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and assume that Φ⁡(𝒙0)−infΦ≤Δ\Phi(\bm{x}^{0})-\inf\Phi\leq\Delta. Since Φ\Phi can be nonsmooth, we seek an ϵ\epsilon-optimization-stationary point (ϵ\epsilon-OS), namely a point 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X} satisfying ‖∇Φ1/(2​ℓ)​(𝒙)‖≤ϵ\|\nabla\Phi_{1/(2\ell)}(\bm{x})\|\leq\epsilon, where Φ1/(2​ℓ)\Phi_{1/(2\ell)} denotes the Moreau envelope of Φ\Phi (Jin et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2020a; Li et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).

We ask how many first-order oracle queries are necessary and sufficient to find an ϵ\epsilon-OS point. Existing first-order approaches include proximal-point methods (Rafique et al., 2022; Thekumparampil et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2020a), two-timescale gradient descent-ascent (GDA) (Lin et al., 2020b), and smoothing methods (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhao, 2024; Li et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2023). With the remaining problem parameters suppressed, the best known upper bounds scale as ϵ−3\epsilon^{-3} up to logarithmic factors. In particular, Minimax-PPA of Lin et al. (2020a) achieves an O⁡(ϵ−3​log2⁡(1/ϵ))O(\epsilon^{-3}\log^{2}(1/\epsilon)) bound, while Perturbed Smoothed FOAM of Li et al. (2026) improves it to O⁡(ϵ−3​log⁡(1/ϵ))O(\epsilon^{-3}\log(1/\epsilon)). These guarantees leave open whether the ϵ−3\epsilon^{-3} dependence is unavoidable for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods in the worst case and whether the remaining logarithmic factor can be removed.

We answer both questions by establishing the optimal deterministic first-order oracle complexity

Θ⁡(ℓ2​D𝒴​Δϵ3)wheneverϵ≲min⁡{ℓ​D𝒴,ℓ​Δ}.\Theta\!\left(\frac{\ell^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta}{\epsilon^{3}}\right)\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad\epsilon\lesssim\min\!\left\{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}},\sqrt{\ell\Delta}\right\}.

The lower bound holds for arbitrary deterministic first-order algorithms. We attain the matching upper bound with Tracked-FOAM, a first-order method that removes the logarithmic factor from previous upper bounds. Thus, the two bounds match in their dependence on ℓ\ell, D𝒴D_{\mathcal{Y}}, Δ\Delta, and ϵ\epsilon throughout the stated regime.

The lower bound must account for the restriction imposed by a bounded dual domain. For nonconvex-strongly-concave (NC-SC) minimax problems with strong concavity parameter μ\mu and condition number κ:=ℓ/μ\kappa:=\ell/\mu, lower bounds of Ω⁡(ℓ​Δ​κ/ϵ2)\Omega(\ell\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}/\epsilon^{2}) are known for zero-respecting first-order algorithms (Li et al., 2021) and linear-span first-order methods (Zhang et al., 2021). Substituting κ≍ℓ2​D𝒴2/ϵ2\kappa\asymp\ell^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}/\epsilon^{2} formally gives the desired NC-C rate. However, those constructions use unbounded dual domains. Restricting the dual variable to a prescribed ball can alter the maximized function and invalidate the gradient lower bound. A separate issue arises from the stationarity criterion: a lower bound on the gradient norm of the value function at a query point does not control the gradient norm of its Moreau envelope, which depends on a proximal point that need not have been queried.

We adapt the construction of Li et al. (2021) by modifying its inner dual chain and introducing a new outer construction. The modified inner chain preserves the zero-chain property, has a smoothness constant independent of its length, and admits an explicit bound on its unconstrained dual maximizer. We replace the standard nonconvex outer chain of Carmon et al. (2020) with outer terms that keep the primal inputs to the inner chains bounded at points in our analysis where the gradient of the value function is small. This ensures that the unconstrained dual maximizer lies inside the prescribed dual ball. The same outer terms also let us extend the lower bound on the gradient norm from the value function to its Moreau envelope. Finally, we adapt the finite-horizon resisting-oracle framework of Carmon et al. (2020, Lemma 7) to our setting to extend the lower bound from zero-respecting first-order algorithms to arbitrary deterministic first-order methods.

We next establish a matching upper bound without logarithmic factors. The framework of Li et al. (2026) combines dual perturbation and primal smoothing to generate a sequence of smooth strongly-convex-strongly-concave (SC-SC) subproblems, each solved by the accelerated FOAM method of Kovalev and Gasnikov (2022). Solving each subproblem to a prescribed accuracy depending on ϵ\epsilon incurs a logarithmic cost at every outer iteration, introducing the remaining logarithmic factor in the overall oracle complexity.

Our Tracked-FOAM method retains the full accelerated FOAM state across successive subproblems. We establish a global Lyapunov descent estimate that jointly controls the gradient norm of the Moreau envelope and the error from approximately solving the SC-SC subproblems with FOAM. This estimate shows that a constant-factor contraction of the FOAM Lyapunov function per outer iteration suffices; the inner solver is never run to an ϵ\epsilon-dependent accuracy, and the logarithmic factor disappears. Consequently, for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, Tracked-FOAM finds an ϵ\epsilon-OS point within

𝒪⁡((ℓ​Δϵ2+1)​max⁡{1,ℓ​D𝒴ϵ})\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{\ell\Delta}{\epsilon^{2}}+1\right)\max\left\{1,\frac{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}}}{\epsilon}\right\}\right)

first-order oracle queries.

Organization.

Section 2 introduces the function class, stationarity criterion, and oracle model, and Section 3 states our main results. Section 4 constructs the hard instance, and Section 5 presents Tracked-FOAM. Section 6 verifies the properties of the hard instance and proves the lower bounds. Section 7 establishes the matching upper bound. Appendix A contains technical lemmas and proofs used in the lower bound analysis. Appendix B describes the implementation of FOAM and proves its contraction and initialization guarantees.

2 Preliminaries

To study Problem (P), we introduce the following class of NC-C functions.

1NC-C function class.

Given ℓ,D𝒴,Δ>0\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta>0, let ℱ⁡(ℓ,D𝒴,Δ)\mathcal{F}(\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta) be the union, over all m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbb{N} and all nonempty closed convex sets 𝒳⊆ℝm\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} and 𝒴⊆ℝn\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} satisfying (𝟎m,𝟎n)∈𝒳×𝒴​ and ​diam⁡(𝒴)≤D𝒴,(\mathbf{0}_{m},\mathbf{0}_{n})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\mbox{ and }\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{Y})\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}, of the class of functions f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying the following properties. For each such function, define Φ⁡(𝐱):=max𝐲∈𝒴⁡f⁡(𝐱,𝐲)+ι𝒳​(𝐱)\Phi(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f(\bm{x};\bm{y})+\iota_{\mathcal{X}}(\bm{x}).

  1. 1.

    (ℓ\ell-smoothness) ff is jointly ℓ\ell-smooth on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, i.e., for all (𝒙1,𝒚1),(𝒙2,𝒚2)∈𝒳×𝒴(\bm{x}_{1},\bm{y}_{1}),(\bm{x}_{2},\bm{y}_{2})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y},

    ‖∇f​(𝒙1,𝒚1)−∇f​(𝒙2,𝒚2)‖≤ℓ⁡‖(𝒙1,𝒚1)−(𝒙2,𝒚2)‖.\left\lVert\nabla f(\bm{x}_{1};\bm{y}_{1})-\nabla f(\bm{x}_{2};\bm{y}_{2})\right\rVert\leq\ell\left\lVert(\bm{x}_{1},\bm{y}_{1})-(\bm{x}_{2},\bm{y}_{2})\right\rVert.
  2. 2.

    (Dual concavity) For every fixed 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}, f⁡(𝒙,⋅)f(\bm{x};\cdot) is concave on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}.

  3. 3.

    (Initial gap) The initialization satisfies Φ⁡(𝟎)−inf𝒙∈𝒳Φ⁡(𝒙)≤Δ.\Phi(\mathbf{0})-\inf_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\Phi(\bm{x})\leq\Delta.

We use the following standard stationarity measure throughout the paper.

2Optimization-stationary point.

Given ϵ>0\epsilon>0, a point 𝐱∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X} is an ϵ\epsilon-optimization-stationary point (ϵ\epsilon-OS) of Problem (P) if

‖∇Φ12​ℓ​(𝒙)‖≤ϵ,\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\frac{1}{2\ell}}(\bm{x})\right\rVert\leq\epsilon,

where Φ1/(2​ℓ)​(𝐱):=min𝐳∈ℝm⁡{Φ⁡(𝐳)+ℓ​∥𝐱−𝐳∥2}\Phi_{1/(2\ell)}(\bm{x}):=\min_{\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\{\Phi(\bm{z})+\ell\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{z}\rVert^{2}\} is the Moreau envelope of Φ\Phi with parameter 1/(2​ℓ)1/(2\ell).

We next introduce the first-order saddle oracle.

3First-order saddle oracle.

For a differentiable function f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}, the first-order saddle oracle at (𝐱,𝐲)∈𝒳×𝒴(\bm{x},\bm{y})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} returns

𝕆f​(𝒙,𝒚):=(f⁡(𝒙,𝒚),∇𝒙f​(𝒙,𝒚),∇𝒚f​(𝒙,𝒚)).\mathbb{O}_{f}(\bm{x};\bm{y}):=\bigl(f(\bm{x};\bm{y}),\nabla_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x};\bm{y}),\nabla_{\bm{y}}f(\bm{x};\bm{y})\bigr).

For a first-order algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} and a differentiable saddle function f:𝒳×𝒴→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}, let 𝖠𝒙(t)​[f]∈𝒳\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(t)}[f]\in\mathcal{X} and 𝖠𝒚(t)​[f]∈𝒴\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(t)}[f]\in\mathcal{Y} denote, respectively, the primal and dual components of its tt-th feasible oracle query. We first consider zero-respecting first-order algorithms that access ff through the oracle 𝕆f\mathbb{O}_{f}.

4Zero-respecting first-order algorithm.

A first-order algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} is zero-respecting if, for each such ff, it starts from (𝖠𝐱(0)​[f],𝖠𝐲(0)​[f])=𝟎(\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(0)}[f],\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(0)}[f])=\mathbf{0} and its query sequence satisfies

supp⁡(𝖠𝒙(t)​[f],𝖠𝒚(t)​[f])⊆⋃s<tsupp⁡(∇𝒙f​(𝖠𝒙(s)​[f],𝖠𝒚(s)​[f]),∇𝒚f​(𝖠𝒙(s)​[f],𝖠𝒚(s)​[f])),∀t≥1.\operatorname{supp}\bigl(\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(t)}[f],\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(t)}[f]\bigr)\subseteq\bigcup_{s<t}\operatorname{supp}\Bigl(\nabla_{\bm{x}}f\bigl(\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(s)}[f];\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(s)}[f]\bigr),\nabla_{\bm{y}}f\bigl(\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(s)}[f];\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(s)}[f]\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad\forall t\geq 1.

We denote the class of such algorithms by 𝒜zr\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{zr}}.

We next define 𝒜det\mathcal{A}_{\det}, the class of deterministic first-order algorithms.

5Deterministic first-order algorithm.

A first-order algorithm 𝖠\mathsf{A} is deterministic if there exists a sequence of maps {Γt}t≥1\{\Gamma_{t}\}_{t\geq 1} such that, for every such ff, it starts from (𝖠𝐱(0)​[f],𝖠𝐲(0)​[f])=𝟎(\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(0)}[f],\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(0)}[f])=\mathbf{0} and its query sequence satisfies

(𝖠𝒙(t)​[f],𝖠𝒚(t)​[f])=Γt​((𝕆f​(𝖠𝒙(s)​[f],𝖠𝒚(s)​[f]))s<t),∀t≥1.\bigl(\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(t)}[f],\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(t)}[f]\bigr)=\Gamma_{t}\left(\Bigl(\mathbb{O}_{f}\bigl(\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(s)}[f];\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(s)}[f]\bigr)\Bigr)_{s<t}\right),\qquad\forall t\geq 1.

We denote the class of such algorithms by 𝒜det\mathcal{A}_{\det}.

We measure the number of oracle queries in the worst case as follows.

6Oracle Complexity.

Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Let 𝒜⊆𝒜det\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{\det} be any nonempty subclass of deterministic first-order algorithms, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a nonempty class of such saddle functions. The oracle complexity of 𝒜\mathcal{A} over ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined by

𝒯ϵ​(𝒜,ℱ):=inf𝖠∈𝒜supf∈ℱinf{t∈ℕ0|𝖠𝒙(t)​[f]​is an ​ϵ​-OS for ​f}.\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{F}):=\inf_{\mathsf{A}\in\mathcal{A}}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\inf\left\{t\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\;\middle|\;\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(t)}[f]\;{\text{is an }\epsilon\text{-OS for }f}\right\}.

To construct the hard instance, we next extend the standard zero-chain structure to the joint primal-dual variable.

7First-order saddle zero-chain.

Let f:𝒳×𝒴⊆ℝm×ℝn→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable, and let 𝛑=(π1,…,πm+n)\bm{\pi}=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{m+n}) be a coordinate ordering of (𝐱,𝐲)(\bm{x},\bm{y}). We say that ff is a first-order saddle zero-chain with respect to 𝛑\bm{\pi} if, for every i∈[m+n]i\in[m+n] and every (𝐱,𝐲)∈𝒳×𝒴(\bm{x},\bm{y})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y},

supp𝝅⁡(𝒙,𝒚)⊆[i−1]⟹supp𝝅⁡(∇𝒙f​(𝒙,𝒚),∇𝒚f​(𝒙,𝒚))⊆[i].\operatorname{supp}_{\bm{\pi}}(\bm{x},\bm{y})\subseteq[i-1]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{supp}_{\bm{\pi}}\bigl(\nabla_{\bm{x}}f(\bm{x};\bm{y}),\nabla_{\bm{y}}f(\bm{x};\bm{y})\bigr)\subseteq[i].

f𝐔,𝐕​(𝒙,𝒚):=f⁡(𝐔⊤​𝒙,𝐕⊤​𝒚).f_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}(\bm{x};\bm{y}):=f(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\bm{x};\mathbf{V}^{\top}\bm{y}).

Let Φ𝐔,𝐕​(𝒙):=max𝒚∈𝔹D𝒴n′⁡f𝐔,𝐕​(𝒙,𝒚)\Phi_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{B}_{D_{\mathcal{Y}}}^{n^{\prime}}}f_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}(\bm{x};\bm{y}) denote its value function.

1Rotation invariance.

Let f∈ℱ⁡(ℓ,D𝒴,Δ)f\in\mathcal{F}(\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta) be defined on ℝm×𝔹D𝒴n\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{B}_{D_{\mathcal{Y}}}^{n}, and let 𝐔∈O⁡(m′,m)\mathbf{U}\in\operatorname{O}(m^{\prime},m) and 𝐕∈O⁡(n′,n)\mathbf{V}\in\operatorname{O}(n^{\prime},n). Then f𝐔,𝐕∈ℱ⁡(ℓ,D𝒴,Δ)f_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}\in\mathcal{F}(\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta). Moreover, for every 𝐱∈ℝm′\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{\prime}},

2Finite-horizon resisting oracle.

For any T0∈ℕT_{0}\in\mathbb{N} and 𝖠∈𝒜det\mathsf{A}\in\mathcal{A}_{\rm det}, there exists a zero-respecting deterministic algorithm 𝖹∈𝒜zr∩𝒜det\mathsf{Z}\in\mathcal{A}_{\rm zr}\cap\mathcal{A}_{\rm det} such that, for every D𝒴>0D_{\mathcal{Y}}>0 and every smooth saddle function f:ℝm×𝔹D𝒴n→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{B}_{D_{\mathcal{Y}}}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, one can find 𝐔∈O⁡(m+T0,m)\mathbf{U}\in\operatorname{O}(m+T_{0},m) and 𝐕∈O⁡(n+T0,n)\mathbf{V}\in\operatorname{O}(n+T_{0},n) satisfying

(𝖹𝒙(t)​[f],𝖹𝒚(t)​[f])=(𝐔⊤​𝖠𝒙(t)​[f𝐔,𝐕],𝐕⊤​𝖠𝒚(t)​[f𝐔,𝐕]),0≤t<T0.\bigl(\mathsf{Z}_{\bm{x}}^{(t)}[f],\mathsf{Z}_{\bm{y}}^{(t)}[f]\bigr)=\bigl(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathsf{A}_{\bm{x}}^{(t)}[f_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}],\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathsf{A}_{\bm{y}}^{(t)}[f_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}]\bigr),\qquad 0\leq t<T_{0}. (2)

3 Main Results

We present lower bounds for deterministic first-order methods and a matching upper bound attained by Tracked-FOAM.

3.1 Lower bound results

We first state the zero-respecting first-order lower bound and then its extension to arbitrary deterministic first-order methods. Both results are proved in Section 6.5.

1Zero-respecting lower bound.

There are numerical constants c0,c1>0c_{0},c_{1}>0 such that, for every ℓ,D𝒴,Δ,ϵ>0\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta,\epsilon>0 satisfying ϵ≤c0​min⁡{ℓ​D𝒴,ℓ​Δ},\epsilon\leq c_{0}\min\{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}},\sqrt{\ell\Delta}\}, there exists an instance f∈ℱ⁡(ℓ,D𝒴,Δ)f\in\mathcal{F}(\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta) for which

𝒯ϵ​(𝒜zr∩𝒜det,{f})≥c1​ℓ2​D𝒴​Δϵ3.\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{\rm zr}\cap\mathcal{A}_{\rm det},\{f\}\bigr)\geq c_{1}\frac{\ell^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta}{\epsilon^{3}}.
2Deterministic lower bound.

There are numerical constants c0,c1>0c_{0},c_{1}>0 such that, for every ℓ,D𝒴,Δ,ϵ>0\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta,\epsilon>0 satisfying ϵ≤c0​min⁡{ℓ​D𝒴,ℓ​Δ},\epsilon\leq c_{0}\min\{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}},\sqrt{\ell\Delta}\}, one has

𝒯ϵ​(𝒜det,ℱ⁡(ℓ,D𝒴,Δ))≥c1​ℓ2​D𝒴​Δϵ3.\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\bigl(\mathcal{A}_{\rm det},\mathcal{F}(\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta)\bigr)\geq c_{1}\frac{\ell^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta}{\epsilon^{3}}.
1Arbitrary deterministic output.

Theorem 2 also covers a deterministic point computed from the final transcript but not previously queried. Indeed, append that primal point, paired with the feasible dual origin, as the algorithm’s next query and apply the lower bound for queried points to the augmented deterministic algorithm.

3.2 Matching upper bound

The following theorem gives our matching upper bound. The algorithm Tracked-FOAM is developed in Section 5.

3Oracle complexity of Tracked-FOAM.

Let ℓ,D𝒴,Δ>0\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta>0 and f∈ℱ⁡(ℓ,D𝒴,Δ)f\in\mathcal{F}(\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta). For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, Algorithm 1, initialized at 𝐳0=𝟎\bm{z}^{0}=\mathbf{0}, returns an ϵ\epsilon-OS point using

𝒪⁡((ℓ​Δϵ2+1)​max⁡{1,ℓ​D𝒴ϵ})\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{\ell\Delta}{\epsilon^{2}}+1\right)\max\left\{1,\frac{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}}}{\epsilon}\right\}\right) (3)

first-order saddle-oracle calls.

2.

In the regime of Theorem 2, the upper bound in (3) simplifies to 𝒪⁡(ℓ2​D𝒴​Δ/ϵ3)\mathcal{O}(\ell^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta/\epsilon^{3}). Thus, Tracked-FOAM is optimal among deterministic first-order methods up to universal constants in this regime.

3Extensions to other stationarity notions and NC-SC problems.

With suitable parameter choices and initialization, Tracked-FOAM also finds an ϵ\epsilon-game-stationary point for NC-C problems, as defined in Li et al. (2026, Definition 2.1 (ii)), with oracle complexity 𝒪(ϵ−5/2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-5/2}). This improves the oracle complexity in Li et al. (2026) by removing the multiplicative log⁡(1/ϵ)\log(1/\epsilon) factor.

For NC-SC problems, where ff is μ\mu-strongly concave in 𝐲\bm{y}, Tracked-FOAM can be configured to find either an ϵ\epsilon-OS point or an ϵ\epsilon-GS point with oracle complexity 𝒪⁡(κ​ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\epsilon^{-2}), where κ:=ℓ/μ\kappa:=\ell/\mu. Zhang et al. (2021) removed the polylogarithmic factors in 1/ϵ1/\epsilon from the bound of Lin et al. (2020a). Our extension further removes the remaining logarithmic factors in the problem parameters, matching the lower bounds of Li et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2021) in its dependence on ϵ\epsilon and κ\kappa.

4 The Construction of Our Hard Instance

In this section, we construct the hard instance used to prove Theorem 1. We first state four properties sufficient for the lower bound and then give an explicit construction.

4.1 Certificates for the hard instance

We begin by providing four properties of the unscaled hard instance sufficient to prove Theorem 1. Call an integer pair (M,N)(M,N) admissible if M≥1M\geq 1 and N≥10N\geq 10. For each admissible pair and each D>0D>0, write the primal variable as 𝒙=(𝒔,𝝂)∈ℝ3​M\bm{x}=(\bm{s},\bm{\nu})\in\mathbb{R}^{3M}, where the state vector 𝒔:=(s1,…,sM)\bm{s}:=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{M}) and the connector vector 𝝂:=(a1,b1,…,aM,bM)\bm{\nu}:=(a_{1},b_{1},\ldots,a_{M},b_{M}). We additionally set s0≡1s_{0}\equiv 1. Let dual coordinates be 𝒚=(𝒚(1),…,𝒚(M)),\bm{y}=(\bm{y}^{(1)},\ldots,\bm{y}^{(M)}), where 𝒚(i)∈ℝN\bm{y}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} for i∈[M]i\in[M].

Define the bounded dual domain 𝒴D:=𝔹DM​N\mathcal{Y}_{D}:=\mathbb{B}_{D}^{MN}, and consider f¯:ℝ3​M×𝒴D→ℝ\bar{f}:\mathbb{R}^{3M}\times\mathcal{Y}_{D}\to\mathbb{R} with coordinate ordering 𝝅\bm{\pi}. Set L:=M⁡(N+3)L:=M(N+3), and denote the corresponding value function by Φ¯​(𝒔,𝝂):=max𝒚∈𝒴D⁡f¯​(𝒔,𝝂,𝒚).\bar{\Phi}(\bm{s},\bm{\nu}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}_{D}}\bar{f}(\bm{s},\bm{\nu};\bm{y}). We impose four conditions on (f¯,𝝅)(\bar{f},\bm{\pi}).

1Unscaled hard instance properties.

There exist numerical constants ℓ0,g0,cΔ,cD>0\ell_{0},g_{0},c_{\Delta},c_{D}>0, independent of M,N,DM,N,D, such that, for every admissible pair (M,N)(M,N) and every D>0D>0, the corresponding unscaled hard instance f¯\bar{f} and coordinate ordering 𝛑\bm{\pi} satisfy the following properties:

  1. (C1)

    The function f¯\bar{f} is jointly ℓ0\ell_{0}-smooth and strongly concave in 𝒚\bm{y}, and its value function Φ¯\bar{\Phi} is differentiable.

  2. (C2)

    The function f¯\bar{f} is a first-order saddle zero-chain with respect to 𝝅\bm{\pi}.

  3. (C3)

    The πL\pi_{L}-th coordinate of (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}) is sMs_{M}. Moreover, whenever N≤cD​DN\leq c_{D}D,

    sM≤15⟹‖∇Φ¯​(𝒔,𝝂)‖≥g0.s_{M}\leq\frac{1}{5}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\left\lVert\nabla\bar{\Phi}(\bm{s},\bm{\nu})\right\rVert\geq g_{0}.
  4. (C4)

    The initial gap of the value function satisfies

    Φ¯​(𝟎,𝟎)−inf(𝒔,𝝂)∈ℝ3​MΦ¯​(𝒔,𝝂)≤cΔ​M.\bar{\Phi}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{0})-\inf_{(\bm{s},\bm{\nu})\in\mathbb{R}^{3M}}\bar{\Phi}(\bm{s},\bm{\nu})\leq c_{\Delta}M.

Conditions 1 (C2) and (C3) force sequential coordinate discovery and rule out small gradients of the value function before the terminal coordinate is reached, provided N≤cD​DN\leq c_{D}D. Conditions 1 (C1) and (C4) allow the instance to be scaled into the target function class.

The bound on the region sM≤1/5s_{M}\leq 1/5 in (C3) also allows us to transfer the lower bound on the gradient norm of the value function to that of its Moreau envelope. After scaling, a sufficiently small gradient norm of the Moreau envelope at a query point with sM=0s_{M}=0 would keep the associated proximal point within the corresponding scaled region. The proximal optimality condition would then contradict the gradient lower bound in (C3).

The remainder of this section constructs a pair (f¯,𝝅)(\bar{f},\bm{\pi}) satisfying these certificates for every admissible pair (M,N)(M,N) and every D>0D>0.

4.2 Overview of the construction

Fix an admissible pair (M,N)(M,N) and D>0D>0. Following Li et al. (2021), we construct MM stages, each containing primal variables (ai,bi,si)(a_{i},b_{i},s_{i}) and a strongly concave inner chain with dual variable 𝒚(i)∈ℝN\bm{y}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. These variables are coupled so that a zero-respecting algorithm must reveal the coordinates of the inner chain before advancing to the next stage. The outer terms are designed to ensure that the gradient of the value function remains bounded away from zero when the final state variable sMs_{M} is small.

The full dual vector is constrained to a Euclidean ball of diameter DD. We therefore also ensure that the unconstrained dual maximizer is feasible at the points used in the argument for the gradient lower bound. At these points, imposing the dual constraint leaves the inner maximum unchanged.

The resulting coordinate order is

𝝅=(a1,y1(1),…,yN(1),b1,s1,…,aM,y1(M),…,yN(M),bM,sM).\bm{\pi}=(a_{1},y_{1}^{(1)},\ldots,y_{N}^{(1)},b_{1},s_{1},\ldots,a_{M},y_{1}^{(M)},\ldots,y_{N}^{(M)},b_{M},s_{M}). (4)

The saddle zero-chain property proved in Section 6 forces sequential discovery along this order, giving a chain length of L=M⁡(N+3)L=M(N+3); see Figure 1.

We next construct the inner chain and then combine it with the outer terms to define the full instance.

4.3 The strongly concave inner chain

We construct an inner chain with primal variables a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} and dual variable 𝒘∈ℝN\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. Its coefficients are chosen so that the inner maximum is a2−a​b+b2a^{2}-ab+b^{2}, independently of NN. The construction adapts the regularized quadratic chain of Li et al. (2021, Section 5.1), which builds on the classical construction of Nesterov (2004). Define

𝐀N:=(1−1−12−1−1⋱⋱⋱2−1−11)∈ℝN×N,𝐌N:=1N2𝐈N+𝐀N,and𝐁N:=𝐌N−1.\mathbf{A}_{N}:=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}1&-1&&&\\ -1&2&-1&&\\ &-1&\ddots&\ddots&\\ &&\ddots&2&-1\\ &&&-1&1\end{array}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N},\quad\mathbf{M}_{N}:=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\mathbf{I}_{N}+\mathbf{A}_{N},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathbf{B}_{N}:=\mathbf{M}_{N}^{-1}.

Since 𝐀N\mathbf{A}_{N} is positive semidefinite, 𝐌N⪰N−2​𝐈N≻0\mathbf{M}_{N}\succeq N^{-2}\mathbf{I}_{N}\succ 0, so 𝐁N\mathbf{B}_{N} is well defined. Set

kN:=(𝐁N)1​N,andcN:=(𝐁N)11kN.k_{N}:=(\mathbf{B}_{N})_{1N},\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad c_{N}:=\frac{(\mathbf{B}_{N})_{11}}{k_{N}}.

The primal variables couple to the two ends of the dual chain: aa interacts with w1w_{1}, and bb with wNw_{N}. Since 𝐌N⪰N−2​𝐈N\mathbf{M}_{N}\succeq N^{-2}\mathbf{I}_{N}, the function H(a,b;⋅)H(a,b;\cdot) is N−2N^{-2}-strongly concave and has the unique maximizer

𝒘⋆​(a,b)=kN−12​𝐁N​(a​𝒆1−b​𝒆N).\bm{w}^{\star}(a,b)=k_{N}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{B}_{N}(a\bm{e}_{1}-b\bm{e}_{N}).

‖𝒘⋆​(a,b)‖≤c𝒚​N​a2+b2,\left\lVert\bm{w}^{\star}(a,b)\right\rVert\leq c_{\bm{y}}N\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}},

4.4 The composite NC-C hard instance

We combine MM copies of the inner chain using three coupling functions and a state regularizer. The entrance and exit couplings connect each inner chain to the adjacent states, while the state coupling and regularizer control the state configuration at points with small gradients. We use a smooth activation function to switch the couplings according to the adjacent states, and bounded extensions of the identity to keep the couplings globally smooth. We first define these auxiliary functions.

Their required bounds are given in Lemmas 14 and 15 in Appendices A.5 and A.6.

5 A Matching Upper-Bound Algorithm

We now develop Tracked-FOAM, which attains the upper bound in Theorem 3. Throughout this section, let f∈ℱ⁡(ℓ,D𝒴,Δ)f\in\mathcal{F}(\ell,D_{\mathcal{Y}},\Delta) with associated feasible sets 𝒳⊆ℝm\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} and 𝒴⊆ℝn\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}.

5.1 Regularized proximal subproblems

Following Li et al. (2026), we add a negative quadratic term in 𝒚\bm{y} and a proximal term in 𝒙\bm{x}. Fix r𝒙:=2​ℓr_{\bm{x}}:=2\ell, let 0<r𝒚≤ℓ/80<r_{\bm{y}}\leq\ell/8, and write r=(r𝒙,r𝒚)r=(r_{\bm{x}},r_{\bm{y}}). Define

fr​(𝒙,𝒚):=f⁡(𝒙,𝒚)−r𝒚2​‖𝒚‖2,and\displaystyle f_{r}(\bm{x};\bm{y}):=f(\bm{x};\bm{y})-\frac{r_{\bm{y}}}{2}\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2},\qquad\mbox{and}
Fr​(𝒙,𝒛,𝒚):=fr​(𝒙,𝒚)+r𝒙2​‖𝒙−𝒛‖2.\displaystyle F_{r}(\bm{x},\bm{z};\bm{y}):=f_{r}(\bm{x};\bm{y})+\frac{r_{\bm{x}}}{2}\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{z}\right\rVert^{2}.

For each 𝒛∈ℝm\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, the function Fr​(⋅,𝒛,⋅)F_{r}(\cdot,\bm{z};\cdot) is ℓ\ell-strongly convex in 𝒙\bm{x} and r𝒚r_{\bm{y}}-strongly concave in 𝒚\bm{y}. Denote its unique saddle point on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} by (𝒙𝒛,r𝒚⋆,𝒚𝒛,r𝒚⋆)(\bm{x}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star},\bm{y}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}).

To relate this subproblem to stationarity, define the regularized value function and its Moreau envelope by

Φr​(𝒙):=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡fr​(𝒙,𝒚)+ι𝒳​(𝒙),and\displaystyle\Phi_{r}(\bm{x}):=\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}f_{r}(\bm{x};\bm{y})+\iota_{\mathcal{X}}(\bm{x}),\qquad\mbox{and}
pr​(𝒛):=min𝒙⁡{Φr​(𝒙)+ℓ​‖𝒙−𝒛‖2}=min𝒙∈𝒳⁡max𝒚∈𝒴​Fr​(𝒙,𝒛,𝒚).\displaystyle p_{r}(\bm{z}):=\min_{\bm{x}}\left\{\Phi_{r}(\bm{x})+\ell\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{z}\right\rVert^{2}\right\}=\min_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}F_{r}(\bm{x},\bm{z};\bm{y}).

The function prp_{r} is continuously differentiable, with gradient given by (13) (Davis and Drusvyatskiy, 2019, Lemma 2.2), i.e.,

𝒙𝒛,r𝒚⋆=prox12​ℓ​Φr⁡(𝒛),and∇pr​(𝒛)=2​ℓ​(𝒛−𝒙𝒛,r𝒚⋆).\bm{x}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}=\operatorname{prox}_{\frac{1}{2\ell}\Phi_{r}}(\bm{z}),\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z})=2\ell(\bm{z}-\bm{x}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}). (13)

Moreover, prp_{r} is 2​ℓ2\ell-smooth (Bauschke and Combettes, 2011, Proposition 12.29).

We next relate ∥∇pr​(𝒛)∥\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z})\rVert to the original OS criterion. The following lemma bounds the difference between ∇pr\nabla p_{r} and ∇Φ1/(2​ℓ)\nabla\Phi_{1/(2\ell)} caused by the dual regularization.

3.

For every r=(2​ℓ,r𝐲)r=(2\ell,r_{\bm{y}}) with r𝐲>0r_{\bm{y}}>0 and every 𝐳∈ℝm\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},

‖∇Φ12​ℓ​(𝒛)−∇pr​(𝒛)‖≤D𝒴​2​ℓ​r𝒚.\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\frac{1}{2\ell}}(\bm{z})-\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z})\right\rVert\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}\sqrt{2\ell r_{\bm{y}}}.
Proof of Lemma 3.

Since 𝟎∈𝒴\mathbf{0}\in\mathcal{Y} and diam⁡(𝒴)≤D𝒴\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{Y})\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}, we have ∥𝒚∥≤D𝒴\lVert\bm{y}\rVert\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}} for every 𝒚∈𝒴\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}. Consequently, for every 𝒙∈𝒳\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X},

0≤Φ⁡(𝒙)−Φr​(𝒙)≤r𝒚2​D𝒴2.0\leq\Phi(\bm{x})-\Phi_{r}(\bm{x})\leq\frac{r_{\bm{y}}}{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}. (14)

Let 𝒙⋆:=proxΦ/(2​ℓ)⁡(𝒛)\bm{x}^{\star}:=\operatorname{prox}_{\Phi/(2\ell)}(\bm{z}) and 𝒙r⋆:=proxΦr/(2​ℓ)⁡(𝒛)\bm{x}_{r}^{\star}:=\operatorname{prox}_{\Phi_{r}/(2\ell)}(\bm{z}). Both Φ\Phi and Φr\Phi_{r} are ℓ\ell-weakly convex, so 𝒙↦Φ⁡(𝒙)+ℓ​∥𝒙−𝒛∥2\bm{x}\mapsto\Phi(\bm{x})+\ell\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{z}\rVert^{2} and 𝒙↦Φr​(𝒙)+ℓ​∥𝒙−𝒛∥2\bm{x}\mapsto\Phi_{r}(\bm{x})+\ell\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{z}\rVert^{2} are ℓ\ell-strongly convex. Applying strong convexity to each function at the minimizer of the other and adding the resulting inequalities gives

ℓ​‖𝒙⋆−𝒙r⋆‖2\displaystyle\ell\left\lVert\bm{x}^{\star}-\bm{x}_{r}^{\star}\right\rVert^{2} ≤[Φ⁡(𝒙r⋆)−Φr​(𝒙r⋆)]−[Φ⁡(𝒙⋆)−Φr​(𝒙⋆)]≤r𝒚2​D𝒴2.\displaystyle\leq[\Phi(\bm{x}_{r}^{\star})-\Phi_{r}(\bm{x}_{r}^{\star})]-[\Phi(\bm{x}^{\star})-\Phi_{r}(\bm{x}^{\star})]\leq\frac{r_{\bm{y}}}{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}.

Consequently,

‖∇Φ12​ℓ​(𝒛)−∇pr​(𝒛)‖=2​ℓ​‖𝒙⋆−𝒙r⋆‖≤D𝒴​2​ℓ​r𝒚.\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{\frac{1}{2\ell}}(\bm{z})-\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z})\right\rVert=2\ell\left\lVert\bm{x}^{\star}-\bm{x}_{r}^{\star}\right\rVert\leq D_{\mathcal{Y}}\sqrt{2\ell r_{\bm{y}}}.

We finish the proof. ∎

For a target accuracy ϵ>0\epsilon>0, set

r𝒚,ϵ:=min⁡{ℓ8,ϵ28​ℓ​D𝒴2}.r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}:=\min\left\{\frac{\ell}{8},\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{8\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}}\right\}. (15)

If 0<r𝒚≤r𝒚,ϵ0<r_{\bm{y}}\leq r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}, Lemma 3 bounds the perturbation error by ϵ/2\epsilon/2. It therefore suffices to find 𝒛∈𝒳\bm{z}\in\mathcal{X} satisfying ∥∇pr​(𝒛)∥≤ϵ/2\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z})\rVert\leq\epsilon/2.

5.2 Approximate proximal points from FOAM

To find a point with small ∥∇pr∥\lVert\nabla p_{r}\rVert, we approximately implement gradient descent on prp_{r}. By (13), an exact gradient step with stepsize 12​ℓ\frac{1}{2\ell} satisfies 𝒛−12​ℓ∇pr(𝒛)=𝒙𝒛,r𝒚⋆.\bm{z}-\frac{1}{2\ell}\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z})=\bm{x}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}. Thus each step amounts to solving the SC-SC subproblem

min𝒙∈𝒳⁡max𝒚∈𝒴​Fr​(𝒙,𝒛,𝒚).\min_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\max_{\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}F_{r}(\bm{x},\bm{z};\bm{y}).

We approximately solve this subproblem using the accelerated FOAM method of Kovalev and Gasnikov (2022), with μx=ℓ\mu_{x}=\ell and μy=r𝒚\mu_{y}=r_{\bm{y}}. Each call provides a primal approximation and an updated solver state, which we retain for the next outer iteration.

For fixed (𝒛,r𝒚)(\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}), FOAM uses a conjugate formulation involving an auxiliary variable 𝝎∈ℝm\bm{\omega}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and the original dual variable 𝒚∈𝒴\bm{y}\in\mathcal{Y}. To describe its iterates and their errors, we first define the associated conjugate objective

P𝒛,r𝒚​(𝝎,𝒚)\displaystyle P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\omega},\bm{y}) :=12​ℓ​‖𝝎‖2+r𝒚2​‖𝒚‖2+ι𝒴​(𝒚)+sup𝒙∈𝒳{⟨𝝎,𝒙⟩−f⁡(𝒙,𝒚)−ℓ​‖𝒙−𝒛‖2+ℓ2​‖𝒙‖2}.\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2\ell}\left\lVert\bm{\omega}\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{r_{\bm{y}}}{2}\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}+\iota_{\mathcal{Y}}(\bm{y})+\sup_{\bm{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\left\{\left\langle\bm{\omega},\bm{x}\right\rangle-f(\bm{x};\bm{y})-\ell\left\lVert\bm{x}-\bm{z}\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{\ell}{2}\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}\right\}.

Let (𝝎𝒛,r𝒚⋆,𝒚𝒛,r𝒚⋆)(\bm{\omega}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star},\bm{y}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}) denote its unique minimizer, and write P𝒛,r𝒚⋆:=min𝝎,𝒚⁡P𝒛,r𝒚​(𝝎,𝒚)P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}:=\min_{\bm{\omega},\bm{y}}P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\omega},\bm{y}). The conjugate and primal solutions satisfy 𝝎𝒛,r𝒚⋆=−ℓ​𝒙𝒛,r𝒚⋆.\bm{\omega}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}=-\ell\bm{x}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}.

The accelerated recursion maintains two pairs of iterates for this conjugate problem: a slow pair (𝝎,𝒚)(\bm{\omega},\bm{y}) and a fast pair (𝝎f,𝒚f)(\bm{\omega}_{f},\bm{y}_{f}). Both pairs target the minimizer (𝝎𝒛,r𝒚⋆,𝒚𝒛,r𝒚⋆)(\bm{\omega}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star},\bm{y}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}) and are retained in the state S=(𝝎,𝒚,𝝎f,𝒚f).S=(\bm{\omega},\bm{y},\bm{\omega}_{f},\bm{y}_{f}). The slow dual variable 𝒚\bm{y} need not belong to 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. The fast pair has finite value under P𝒛,r𝒚P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}, so 𝒚f∈𝒴\bm{y}_{f}\in\mathcal{Y}. All calls to the first-order saddle oracle are made at feasible points in 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}; see Appendix B.1.

The fast pair provides the primal approximation

𝒛+:=proj𝒳(−𝝎f/ℓ).\bm{z}^{+}:=\proj_{\mathcal{X}}(-\bm{\omega}_{f}/\ell).

We use a Lyapunov function to measure the error in both pairs and bound the distance from 𝒛+\bm{z}^{+} to 𝒙𝒛,r𝒚⋆\bm{x}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}. Set αr𝒚:=8​r𝒚/ℓ≤1\alpha_{r_{\bm{y}}}:=\sqrt{8r_{\bm{y}}/\ell}\leq 1. We use αr𝒚\alpha_{r_{\bm{y}}} times the Lyapunov function in Kovalev and Gasnikov (2022, Supplement, Lemma 7), specialized to Fr​(⋅,𝒛,⋅)F_{r}(\cdot,\bm{z};\cdot):

ℒ𝒛,r𝒚​(S)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S) :=2​αr𝒚ℓ​‖𝝎−𝝎𝒛,r𝒚⋆‖2+2​r𝒚​‖𝒚−𝒚𝒛,r𝒚⋆‖2+2​(P𝒛,r𝒚​(𝝎f,𝒚f)−P𝒛,r𝒚⋆).\displaystyle:=\frac{2\alpha_{r_{\bm{y}}}}{\ell}\left\lVert\bm{\omega}-\bm{\omega}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}\right\rVert^{2}+2r_{\bm{y}}\left\lVert\bm{y}-\bm{y}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}\right\rVert^{2}+2\left(P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\omega}_{f},\bm{y}_{f})-P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}\right). (16)

The first two terms measure the error of the slow pair (𝝎,𝒚)(\bm{\omega},\bm{y}), while the last term measures the suboptimality of the fast pair (𝝎f,𝒚f)(\bm{\omega}_{f},\bm{y}_{f}) in the conjugate objective.

For fixed (𝒛,r𝒚)(\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}), a call to FOAM takes an initial state SS with ℒ𝒛,r𝒚​(S)<∞\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S)<\infty and a target error reduction factor ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). It runs a prescribed number of iterations and returns

S+=(𝝎+,𝒚+,𝝎f+,𝒚f+):=FOAM𝒛,r𝒚​(S,ρ).S^{+}=(\bm{\omega}^{+},\bm{y}^{+},\bm{\omega}_{f}^{+},\bm{y}_{f}^{+}):=\textnormal{{FOAM}}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S;\rho).

The corresponding primal output is proj𝒳(−𝝎f+/ℓ)\proj_{\mathcal{X}}(-\bm{\omega}_{f}^{+}/\ell). The iteration count is chosen to reduce ℒ𝒛,r𝒚\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}} by a factor of ρ\rho. The following lemma gives the primal approximation error, the reduction in the Lyapunov function, and the oracle cost.

4FOAM contraction and primal approximation bound.

For every 𝐳∈𝒳\bm{z}\in\mathcal{X}, 0<r𝐲≤ℓ/80<r_{\bm{y}}\leq\ell/8, and every state SS with ℒ𝐳,r𝐲​(S)<∞\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S)<\infty,

ℓ​‖proj𝒳⁡(−𝝎fℓ)−𝒙𝒛,r𝒚⋆‖2≤ℒ𝒛,r𝒚​(S).\ell\left\lVert\proj_{\mathcal{X}}\left(-\frac{\bm{\omega}_{f}}{\ell}\right)-\bm{x}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}\right\rVert^{2}\leq\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S). (17)

Moreover, for every ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1),

ℒ𝒛,r𝒚​(FOAM𝒛,r𝒚​(S,ρ))≤ρ​ℒ𝒛,r𝒚​(S),\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}\left(\textnormal{{FOAM}}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S;\rho)\right)\leq\rho\,\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S), (18)

and the call requires 𝒪⁡(1+ℓ/r𝐲​log⁡(1/ρ))\mathcal{O}(1+\sqrt{\ell/r_{\bm{y}}}\log(1/\rho)) first-order saddle-oracle calls.

The proof of Lemma 4, the iteration count, and the implementation using feasible oracle queries are given in Appendix B. The call does not require evaluating ℒ𝒛,r𝒚\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}, which depends on the unknown minimizer and optimal value of P𝒛,r𝒚P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}. For a fixed numerical ρ\rho, reducing the error by this factor requires 𝒪⁡(ℓ/r𝒚)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ell/r_{\bm{y}}}) oracle calls.

These guarantees apply to a fixed subproblem. In the next subsection, we show how to update the state when 𝒛\bm{z} changes and control its error for the new subproblem.

5.3 Tracking across successive subproblems

Each outer iteration changes the proximal center and hence the SC-SC subproblem. To reuse the previous FOAM state, we first examine how this change affects the subproblem.

Fix 0<r𝒚≤ℓ/80<r_{\bm{y}}\leq\ell/8 in this subsection and consider two proximal centers 𝒛,𝒛′∈𝒳\bm{z},\bm{z}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}. Write 𝒅:=𝒛′−𝒛\bm{d}:=\bm{z}^{\prime}-\bm{z} for their difference. Expanding the proximal term gives

Fr​(𝒙,𝒛′,𝒚)=Fr​(𝒙,𝒛,𝒚)−2​ℓ​⟨𝒅,𝒙⟩+ℓ⁡(‖𝒛′‖2−‖𝒛‖2).F_{r}(\bm{x},\bm{z}^{\prime};\bm{y})=F_{r}(\bm{x},\bm{z};\bm{y})-2\ell\left\langle\bm{d},\bm{x}\right\rangle+\ell\bigl(\left\lVert\bm{z}^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}-\left\lVert\bm{z}\right\rVert^{2}\bigr). (19)

The last term is independent of (𝒙,𝒚)(\bm{x},\bm{y}). In the supremum defining P𝒛′,r𝒚P_{\bm{z}^{\prime},r_{\bm{y}}}, the resulting linear term is canceled by replacing 𝝎\bm{\omega} with 𝝎−2​ℓ​𝒅\bm{\omega}-2\ell\bm{d}. We therefore translate both conjugate variables in the retained state:

S~:=(𝝎−2​ℓ​𝒅,𝒚,𝝎f−2​ℓ​𝒅,𝒚f).\widetilde{S}:=\left(\bm{\omega}-2\ell\bm{d},\,\bm{y},\,\bm{\omega}_{f}-2\ell\bm{d},\,\bm{y}_{f}\right). (20)

The following proposition bounds the error of this state for the new subproblem.

1.

For every 𝐳,𝐳′∈𝒳\bm{z},\bm{z}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X} with 𝐳′=𝐳+𝐝\bm{z}^{\prime}=\bm{z}+\bm{d} and every state SS with ℒ𝐳,r𝐲​(S)<∞\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S)<\infty, the translated state in (20) satisfies

ℒ𝒛′,r𝒚​(S~)≤2​ℒ𝒛,r𝒚​(S)+24​ℓ​‖𝒅‖2.\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z}^{\prime},r_{\bm{y}}}(\widetilde{S})\leq 2\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S)+24\ell\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert^{2}. (21)

Consequently, for every ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1),

ℒ𝒛′,r𝒚​(FOAM𝒛′,r𝒚​(S~,ρ))≤ρ⁡(2​ℒ𝒛,r𝒚​(S)+24​ℓ​‖𝒅‖2).\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z}^{\prime},r_{\bm{y}}}\left(\textnormal{{FOAM}}_{\bm{z}^{\prime},r_{\bm{y}}}(\widetilde{S};\rho)\right)\leq\rho\left(2\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S)+24\ell\left\lVert\bm{d}\right\rVert^{2}\right). (22)

The proof of Proposition 1 is given in Section 7.1. This estimate allows us to bound the error for the new subproblem using the previous error bound and the displacement 𝒅\bm{d}. We use it to maintain a computable upper bound BtB^{t} satisfying ℒ𝒛t,r𝒚​(St)≤Bt.\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z}^{t},r_{\bm{y}}}(S^{t})\leq B^{t}.

Suppose that this bound holds at iteration tt, and write St=(𝝎t,𝒚t,𝝎ft,𝒚ft)S^{t}=(\bm{\omega}^{t},\bm{y}^{t},\bm{\omega}_{f}^{t},\bm{y}_{f}^{t}). We first take the approximate proximal step provided by StS^{t}:

𝒛t+1:=proj𝒳(−𝝎ft/ℓ),and𝒅t:=𝒛t+1−𝒛t.\bm{z}^{t+1}:=\proj_{\mathcal{X}}(-\bm{\omega}_{f}^{t}/\ell),\quad\text{and}\quad\bm{d}^{t}:=\bm{z}^{t+1}-\bm{z}^{t}.

To obtain an initial state for the subproblem at 𝒛t+1\bm{z}^{t+1}, we translate StS^{t} as in (20):

S~t:=(𝝎t−2​ℓ​𝒅t,𝒚t,𝝎ft−2​ℓ​𝒅t,𝒚ft).\widetilde{S}^{t}:=\left(\bm{\omega}^{t}-2\ell\bm{d}^{t},\,\bm{y}^{t},\,\bm{\omega}_{f}^{t}-2\ell\bm{d}^{t},\,\bm{y}_{f}^{t}\right).

Starting from S~t\widetilde{S}^{t}, we run the prescribed number of FOAM iterations to reduce the Lyapunov function for this subproblem by a factor of 1/4001/400, and denote the returned state by St+1:=FOAM𝒛t+1,r𝒚​(S~t,1/400).S^{t+1}:=\textnormal{{FOAM}}_{\bm{z}^{t+1},r_{\bm{y}}}(\widetilde{S}^{t};{1}/{400}). We update this computable error bound accordingly:

Bt+1:=1400​(2​Bt+24​ℓ​‖𝒅t‖2).B^{t+1}:=\frac{1}{400}\left(2B^{t}+24\ell\left\lVert\bm{d}^{t}\right\rVert^{2}\right). (23)

Proposition 1 then gives ℒ𝒛t+1,r𝒚​(St+1)≤Bt+1.\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z}^{t+1},r_{\bm{y}}}(S^{t+1})\leq B^{t+1}. Thus the same error bound is maintained at the next iteration, using only BtB^{t} and the computed displacement 𝒅t\bm{d}^{t}.

For the fixed reduction factor 1/4001/400, Lemma 4 gives an oracle cost of 𝒪⁡(ℓ/r𝒚)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ell/r_{\bm{y}}}) per outer iteration. The Lyapunov descent estimate in Section 7 justifies this choice of reduction factor.

5.4 The Tracked-FOAM algorithm

We now explain why the updates in Section 5.3 suffice to find an ϵ\epsilon-OS point. The primal error bound in Lemma 4 and the bound maintained in Section 5.3 give

ℓ​‖𝒛t+1−𝒙𝒛t,r𝒚⋆‖2≤ℒ𝒛t,r𝒚​(St)≤Bt.\ell\left\lVert\bm{z}^{t+1}-\bm{x}_{\bm{z}^{t},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}\right\rVert^{2}\leq\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z}^{t},r_{\bm{y}}}(S^{t})\leq B^{t}.

Using the 2​ℓ2\ell-smoothness of prp_{r}, we therefore obtain

pr​(𝒛t+1)−pr​(𝒛t)\displaystyle p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t+1})-p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t}) ≤−‖∇pr​(𝒛t)‖24​ℓ+ℓ​‖𝒛t+1−𝒙𝒛t,r𝒚⋆‖2\displaystyle\leq-\frac{\left\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t})\right\rVert^{2}}{4\ell}+\ell\left\lVert\bm{z}^{t+1}-\bm{x}_{\bm{z}^{t},r_{\bm{y}}}^{\star}\right\rVert^{2}
≤−‖∇pr​(𝒛t)‖24​ℓ+Bt.\displaystyle\leq-\frac{\left\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t})\right\rVert^{2}}{4\ell}+B^{t}. (24)

The negative term is the decrease from an exact gradient step, while BtB^{t} bounds the additional error from approximately solving the subproblem. To control its accumulated contribution, we combine this inequality with the update of BtB^{t} in (23) and define

Wt:=pr​(𝒛t)+2​Bt.W^{t}:=p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t})+2B^{t}. (25)

With the reduction factor 1/4001/400 used in the FOAM calls, combining (24) with (23) yields

Wt+1−Wt≤−34​(‖∇pr​(𝒛t)‖24​ℓ+Bt).W^{t+1}-W^{t}\leq-\frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{\left\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t})\right\rVert^{2}}{4\ell}+B^{t}\right).

This estimate controls both the gradient norm of prp_{r} and the error from approximately solving the subproblems. Thus reducing the FOAM Lyapunov function by a factor of 1/4001/400 at each outer iteration suffices to obtain a small gradient norm. By Lemma 4, each call costs 𝒪⁡(ℓ/r𝒚)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ell/r_{\bm{y}}}) oracle queries. The proof of the descent estimate is given in Lemma 10.

The iteration bound depends on the initial Lyapunov gap W0−infprW^{0}-\inf p_{r}, which includes the initial error bound 2​B02B^{0}. We therefore initialize FOAM with an error bound B0B^{0} of order Δ+r𝒚​D𝒴2\Delta+r_{\bm{y}}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}. Keeping 𝒛0=𝟎\bm{z}^{0}=\mathbf{0} fixed, we start with r𝒚=ℓ/8r_{\bm{y}}=\ell/8 and successively divide r𝒚r_{\bm{y}} by four. After each decrease, we run FOAM from the state obtained at the preceding level. We stop at the first level satisfying r𝒚≤r𝒚,ϵr_{\bm{y}}\leq r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}, where r𝒚,ϵr_{\bm{y},\epsilon} is defined in (15). The following proposition bounds the error of the resulting state and the total initialization cost.

2Warm-start initialization.

Let 𝐳0=𝟎\bm{z}^{0}=\mathbf{0}. The initialization constructs a dual regularization parameter r𝐲r_{\bm{y}} and a FOAM state S0S^{0} satisfying

ℒ𝒛0,r𝒚​(S0)≤15​(Δ+r𝒚​D𝒴2)andr𝒚,ϵ4<r𝒚≤r𝒚,ϵ.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z}^{0},r_{\bm{y}}}(S^{0})\leq 15\left(\Delta+r_{\bm{y}}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\right)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\frac{r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}}{4}<r_{\bm{y}}\leq r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}. (26)

The construction requires 𝒪⁡(ℓ/r𝐲)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ell/r_{\bm{y}}}) first-order saddle-oracle calls.

We set B0:=15​(Δ+r𝒚​D𝒴2).B^{0}:=15\left(\Delta+r_{\bm{y}}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\right). Proposition 2 ensures that ℒ𝒛0,r𝒚​(S0)≤B0\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z}^{0},r_{\bm{y}}}(S^{0})\leq B^{0}, providing the initial error bound required by Section 5.3. We then keep r𝒚r_{\bm{y}} fixed and apply the updates described there. The full initialization and its proof are given in Section 7.2. The cost bounds for the successive initialization levels grow geometrically, so their sum is dominated by the final level. Hence initialization introduces no additional logarithmic factor.

To select the output, we use

Qt:=ℓ​‖𝒛t+1−𝒛t‖2+Bt.Q^{t}:=\ell\left\lVert\bm{z}^{t+1}-\bm{z}^{t}\right\rVert^{2}+B^{t}.

The first term measures the computed step, while the second accounts for the error in approximating the exact proximal point. Lemma 11 shows that

‖∇pr​(𝒛t)‖2≤8​ℓ​Qt,andmin0≤t<T⁡Qt≤4T​(W0−infpr).\left\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t})\right\rVert^{2}\leq 8\ell Q^{t},\quad\text{and}\quad\min_{0\leq t<T}Q^{t}\leq\frac{4}{T}\left(W^{0}-\inf p_{r}\right).

Thus a small value of QtQ^{t} certifies a small gradient norm, and the descent estimate guarantees that such an iterate exists. We return the iterate with the smallest value of QtQ^{t}, choosing the smallest index in case of a tie. Algorithm 1 gives the complete method.

6 Proof of the Lower Bounds

We verify Conditions 1 (C1)-(C4) for the instance constructed in Section 4. We then scale the instance and prove Theorems 1 and 2.

6.1 Smoothness and dual concavity

We begin with the properties required by Condition 1 (C1).

3.

There is a numerical constant ℓ0>0\ell_{0}>0, independent of M,N,DM,N,D, such that f¯\bar{f} is jointly ℓ0\ell_{0}-smooth and N−2N^{-2}-strongly concave in 𝐲\bm{y}. Proof of Proposition 3.

For each i∈[M]i\in[M], let BiB_{i} denote the ii-th summand in (11). Lemma 13 shows that the first two derivatives of pp are uniformly bounded. Lemmas 14 and 15 show that qq, e𝒔e_{\bm{s}}, and e𝝂e_{\bm{\nu}}, together with their first two derivatives, are uniformly bounded by numerical constants. Applying the product and chain rules to (7)-(9) and (10) therefore gives uniform Hessian bounds for CenC_{\rm en}, CexC_{\rm ex}, CstC_{\rm st}, and RR. Lemma 12 (ii) also gives a uniform Hessian bound for HH. Thus each BiB_{i} is jointly ℓB\ell_{B}-smooth for a numerical constant ℓB>0\ell_{B}>0 independent of M,N,DM,N,D.

Since BiB_{i} and BjB_{j} depend on disjoint coordinates whenever |i−j|≥2|i-j|\geq 2, the sum over odd indices and the sum over even indices each have a block diagonal Hessian with norm at most ℓB\ell_{B}. Their sum f¯\bar{f} is therefore jointly ℓ0\ell_{0}-smooth with ℓ0:=2​ℓB\ell_{0}:=2\ell_{B}.

Only the inner chains depend on 𝒚\bm{y}. By Lemma 12 (ii), each is N−2N^{-2}-strongly concave in its own dual coordinates. Since these coordinates are disjoint, f¯\bar{f} is N−2N^{-2}-strongly concave in 𝒚\bm{y}. 7 Proof of the Upper Bound

We prove Theorem 3 in three steps. First, we establish Proposition 1, which bounds the error of the translated FOAM state. Next, we prove Proposition 2 by constructing an initial state through successive reductions of the dual regularization parameter. Finally, we combine these bounds with the outer updates to establish descent, stationarity, and the oracle complexity. The implementation of FOAM using feasible queries and the initialization at the first regularization level are given in Appendices B.1 and B.2, respectively.

‖∇pr​(𝒛t⋆)‖2≤992​ℓT​(Δ+r𝒚​D𝒴2).\left\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t^{\star}})\right\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{992\ell}{T}\left(\Delta+r_{\bm{y}}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\right).

Since r𝒚≤r𝒚,ϵr_{\bm{y}}\leq r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}, we have r𝒚​D𝒴2≤ϵ2/(8​ℓ)r_{\bm{y}}D_{\mathcal{Y}}^{2}\leq\epsilon^{2}/(8\ell). By the choice of TT in Algorithm 1,

‖∇pr​(𝒛t⋆)‖2≤992T​(ℓ​Δ+ϵ28)≤9924000​ϵ2<ϵ24.\left\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t^{\star}})\right\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{992}{T}\left(\ell\Delta+\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{8}\right)\leq\frac{992}{4000}\epsilon^{2}<\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{4}.

Thus ∥∇pr​(𝒛t⋆)∥<ϵ/2\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t^{\star}})\rVert<\epsilon/2. The same bound r𝒚≤r𝒚,ϵr_{\bm{y}}\leq r_{\bm{y},\epsilon} gives D𝒴​2​ℓ​r𝒚≤ϵ/2D_{\mathcal{Y}}\sqrt{2\ell r_{\bm{y}}}\leq\epsilon/2. Lemma 3 therefore implies

‖∇Φ1/(2​ℓ)​(𝒛t⋆)‖≤‖∇pr​(𝒛t⋆)‖+D𝒴​2​ℓ​r𝒚≤ϵ.\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{1/(2\ell)}(\bm{z}^{t^{\star}})\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\nabla p_{r}(\bm{z}^{t^{\star}})\right\rVert+D_{\mathcal{Y}}\sqrt{2\ell r_{\bm{y}}}\leq\epsilon.

Since 𝒛t⋆∈𝒳\bm{z}^{t^{\star}}\in\mathcal{X}, the selected output is an ϵ\epsilon-OS point.

Finally, we count the calls to the first-order saddle oracle. By Lemma 4, each FOAM call in the outer iterations requires 𝒪⁡(ℓ/r𝒚)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ell/r_{\bm{y}}}) oracle calls, since its reduction factor is fixed at 1/4001/400. Proposition 2 gives the same order of cost for the initialization. Moreover, r𝒚>r𝒚,ϵ/4r_{\bm{y}}>r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}/4 implies

ℓr𝒚=𝒪⁡(ℓr𝒚,ϵ)=𝒪⁡(max⁡{1,ℓ​D𝒴ϵ}).\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{r_{\bm{y}}}}=\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{r_{\bm{y},\epsilon}}}\right)=\mathcal{O}\left(\max\left\{1,\frac{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}}}{\epsilon}\right\}\right).

Since T=𝒪⁡(ℓ​Δ/ϵ2+1)T=\mathcal{O}(\ell\Delta/\epsilon^{2}+1), the initialization and the TT outer iterations together require

𝒪⁡((T+1)​ℓr𝒚)=𝒪⁡[(ℓ​Δϵ2+1)​max⁡{1,ℓ​D𝒴ϵ}]\mathcal{O}\left((T+1)\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{r_{\bm{y}}}}\right)=\mathcal{O}\left[\left(\frac{\ell\Delta}{\epsilon^{2}}+1\right)\max\left\{1,\frac{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}}}{\epsilon}\right\}\right]

calls to the first-order saddle oracle. This proves Theorem 3. ∎

8 Conclusion

We established the optimal deterministic first-order oracle complexity of finding an ϵ\epsilon-OS point in smooth NC-C minimax optimization with a compact convex dual domain. For ϵ≲min⁡{ℓ​D𝒴,ℓ​Δ}\epsilon\lesssim\min\{\ell D_{\mathcal{Y}},\sqrt{\ell\Delta}\}, we proved a lower bound of Ω⁡(ℓ2​D𝒴​Δ/ϵ3)\Omega(\ell^{2}D_{\mathcal{Y}}\Delta/\epsilon^{3}) for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods. Our algorithm, Tracked-FOAM, attains the matching upper bound, thereby removing the logarithmic gap in previous complexity guarantees.

A natural next step is to extend our lower bound to randomized first-order algorithms and determine whether randomization can improve the worst-case oracle complexity. Our C∞C^{\infty} hard instance may also serve as a starting point for establishing higher-order oracle lower bounds, extending the study of such bounds for smooth nonconvex minimization (Carmon et al., 2020) to the minimax setting. This direction requires controlling the higher-order derivatives and the information they reveal about the hard instance.

A.3 Properties of the inner chain

The following lemma adapts Li et al. [2021, Lemmas 4 and 7] to our setting and records the properties of the inner chain used in Section 6.

12Properties of the inner chain.

There are numerical constants cH,c𝐲>0c_{H},c_{\bm{y}}>0, independent of M,N,DM,N,D, such that the following properties hold.

  1. (i)

    The bound 6/5≤cN≤8/56/5\leq c_{N}\leq 8/5 and the identity (5) hold. Moreover, the maximizer satisfies ∥𝒘⋆​(a,b)∥≤c𝒚​N​a2+b2\lVert\bm{w}^{\star}(a,b)\rVert\leq c_{\bm{y}}N\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}.

  2. (ii)

    The function H(a,b;⋅)H(a,b;\cdot) is N−2N^{-2}-strongly concave and its joint Hessian has norm at most cHc_{H};

Appendix B Technical Details of FOAM

This appendix presents an implementation of FOAM using feasible oracle queries and proves Lemma 4. It also constructs the state at the first regularization level used in the geometric initialization. The stability estimate is proved in Section 7.1, and the geometric initialization is analyzed in Section 7.2. Throughout, r=(2​ℓ,r𝒚)r=(2\ell,r_{\bm{y}}), and P𝒛,r𝒚P_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}} and ℒ𝒛,r𝒚\mathcal{L}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}} denote the conjugate objective and Lyapunov function defined in the main text.

B.1 Feasible implementation and contraction of FOAM

Fix a proximal center 𝒛∈𝒳\bm{z}\in\mathcal{X} and a dual regularization parameter 0<r𝒚≤ℓ/80<r_{\bm{y}}\leq\ell/8, and define

F^𝒛​(𝒙,𝒚):=Fr​(𝒙,𝒛,𝒚)−ℓ2​‖𝒙‖2+r𝒚2​‖𝒚‖2.\widehat{F}_{\bm{z}}(\bm{x};\bm{y}):=F_{r}(\bm{x},\bm{z};\bm{y})-\frac{\ell}{2}\left\lVert\bm{x}\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{r_{\bm{y}}}{2}\left\lVert\bm{y}\right\rVert^{2}.

The function F^𝒛\widehat{F}_{\bm{z}} is convex in 𝒙\bm{x}, concave in 𝒚\bm{y}, and independent of r𝒚r_{\bm{y}}.

Given (𝝎g,𝒚g)∈ℝm×ℝn(\bm{\omega}_{g},\bm{y}_{g})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}, a relative-prox output is a tuple (𝒙f,𝒚f+,𝝎f+,𝒘f+)∈𝒳×𝒴×ℝm×ℝn(\bm{x}_{f},\bm{y}_{f}^{+},\bm{\omega}_{f}^{+},\bm{w}_{f}^{+})\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} satisfying the conditions below. Define

𝚫x\displaystyle\bm{\Delta}_{x} :=𝝎f++ℓ2​(𝒙f−ℓ−1​𝝎g),and\displaystyle:=\bm{\omega}_{f}^{+}+\frac{\ell}{2}(\bm{x}_{f}-\ell^{-1}\bm{\omega}_{g}),\qquad\mbox{and}
𝚫y\displaystyle\bm{\Delta}_{y} :=𝒘f++r𝒚​𝒚f++ℓ8​(𝒚f+−𝒚g).\displaystyle:=\bm{w}_{f}^{+}+r_{\bm{y}}\bm{y}_{f}^{+}+\frac{\ell}{8}(\bm{y}_{f}^{+}-\bm{y}_{g}).

We require

𝝎f+−∇𝒙Fr​(𝒙f,𝒛,𝒚f+)+ℓ​𝒙f∈N𝒳​(𝒙f),\displaystyle\bm{\omega}_{f}^{+}-\nabla_{\bm{x}}F_{r}(\bm{x}_{f},\bm{z};\bm{y}_{f}^{+})+\ell\bm{x}_{f}\in N_{\mathcal{X}}(\bm{x}_{f}), (62)
𝒘f++∇𝒚Fr​(𝒙f,𝒛,𝒚f+)+r𝒚​𝒚f+∈N𝒴​(𝒚f+),and\displaystyle\bm{w}_{f}^{+}+\nabla_{\bm{y}}F_{r}(\bm{x}_{f},\bm{z};\bm{y}_{f}^{+})+r_{\bm{y}}\bm{y}_{f}^{+}\in N_{\mathcal{Y}}(\bm{y}_{f}^{+}),\qquad\mbox{and} (63)
8ℓ​‖𝚫x‖2+8ℓ​‖𝚫y‖2≤ℓ8​‖𝒙f+ℓ−1​𝝎g‖2+ℓ8​‖𝒚f+−𝒚g‖2.\displaystyle\frac{8}{\ell}\left\lVert\bm{\Delta}_{x}\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{8}{\ell}\left\lVert\bm{\Delta}_{y}\right\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{\ell}{8}\left\lVert\bm{x}_{f}+\ell^{-1}\bm{\omega}_{g}\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{\ell}{8}\left\lVert\bm{y}_{f}^{+}-\bm{y}_{g}\right\rVert^{2}. (64)

These are the relative-prox conditions in Kovalev and Gasnikov [2022, Condition (18)], with μx=ℓ\mu_{x}=\ell, μy=r𝒚\mu_{y}=r_{\bm{y}}, θy=8/ℓ\theta_{y}=8/\ell, and indicator regularizers ι𝒳\iota_{\mathcal{X}} and ι𝒴\iota_{\mathcal{Y}}.

For the FOAM update, set αr𝒚:=8​r𝒚/ℓ\alpha_{r_{\bm{y}}}:=\sqrt{8r_{\bm{y}}/\ell}, ηω:=ℓ/2\eta_{\omega}:=\ell/2, and ηy:=4/(αr𝒚​ℓ)\eta_{y}:=4/(\alpha_{r_{\bm{y}}}\ell). Algorithm 2 maps the current state SS to the next state S+S^{+}.

For ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1), define

Kρ:=⌈2αr𝒚​log⁡1ρ⌉.K_{\rho}:=\left\lceil\frac{2}{\alpha_{r_{\bm{y}}}}\log\frac{1}{\rho}\right\rceil.

We write FOAM𝒛,r𝒚​(S,ρ)\textnormal{{FOAM}}_{\bm{z},r_{\bm{y}}}(S;\rho) for the state obtained after KρK_{\rho} applications of Algorithm 2.

To compute the relative-prox output using only feasible queries, we use the projected iterations in Algorithm 3. Set γ:=8/ℓ\gamma:=8/\ell and define
